title: Obadiah 1:10–14
context: The LORD names the reason for Edom’s judgment: violence done to its brother Jacob. The language of brotherhood recalls Jacob and Esau (Genesis 25:23; 27:41) and the law’s instruction not to abhor an Edomite, for he is your brother (Deuteronomy 23:7; compare Numbers 20:14–21). On the day strangers carried off Jerusalem’s wealth and cast lots for the city, Edom stood aloof and was like one of them. A series of commands follows: do not gloat over your brother in his disaster, do not rejoice over Judah’s destruction, do not enter the gate of the LORD’s people, seize their wealth, or stand at the crossroads to cut off or hand over survivors. Many read these lines as describing what Edom did, addressed vividly as though it were happening. Psalm 137:7, Lamentations 4:21–22, Ezekiel 35:5, 15, and Joel 3:19 speak of Edom’s hostility in similar terms. The Jacob and Esau background is sometimes connected with Malachi 1:2–3 and Romans 9:13; readers who want the Arminian and Reformed readings of that line can see the Romans 9:13 box, while here the focus is on Edom’s treatment of a brother in distress. Shared ground: both traditions generally read the passage as a warning against gloating, cruelty, and betrayal of those in need (compare Proverbs 24:17).

verses.text: For the violence done to your brother Jacob, shame will cover you, and you will be cut off forever.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD naming violence against brother Jacob as the reason for Edom’s shame. Betraying a brother is grave.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the history of Jacob and Esau in the background (compare Genesis 27:41; Amos 1:11). Shared ground: both traditions generally read the verse as condemning cruelty toward kin.

verses.text: In the day that you stood on the other side, in the day that strangers carried away his substance and foreigners entered into his gates and cast lots for Jerusalem, even you were like one of them.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Edom standing aloof while strangers plundered Jerusalem, becoming like one of them. Standing by is itself a choice.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see complicity in the suffering of others as real guilt. Shared ground: both traditions generally read the verse as a warning that passive cruelty shares in the wrong done.

verses.text: But don’t look down on your brother in the day of his disaster, and don’t rejoice over the children of Judah in the day of their destruction. Don’t speak proudly in the day of distress.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see commands not to gloat over a brother in his disaster or rejoice over Judah’s destruction. Malicious joy is condemned.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the heart’s pleasure in another’s ruin exposed (compare Proverbs 24:17; 1 Corinthians 13:6). Shared ground: both traditions generally read the verse as a lasting moral warning.

verses.text: Don’t enter into the gate of my people in the day of their calamity. Don’t look down on their affliction in the day of their calamity, neither seize their wealth on the day of their calamity.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see commands not to enter the gate of the LORD’s people, look down on their affliction, or seize their wealth. Exploiting the suffering is forbidden.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the repeated phrase in the day of their calamity emphasizing Edom’s cruelty. Shared ground: both traditions generally read the verse as condemning profit from others’ distress.

verses.text: Don’t stand in the crossroads to cut off those of his who escape. Don’t deliver up those of his who remain in the day of distress.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see commands not to stand at the crossroads to cut off or hand over survivors. Betraying refugees is especially grievous.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the final and most serious charge in the list. Shared ground: both traditions generally read the verse as a sober call to protect, not exploit, those who flee.
